# atoi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/atoi/

## Expand description

A crate for parsing integers directly from ASCII (`[u8]`) without encoding them into utf8
first. The name is inspired by the famous C function.

Using `str::from_utf8` and `str::parse`
is likely to be more idiomatic. Use this crate if you want to avoid decoding bytes into utf8
(e.g. for performance reasons).

Note that if you want to know how much of the input has been used, you can use the
`FromRadix10` trait, for example:

```
use atoi::FromRadix10;
/// Return the parsed integer and remaining slice if successful.
fn atoi_with_rest<I: FromRadix10>(text: &[u8]) -> ((&[u8], Option<I>)) {
    match I::from_radix_10(text) {
        (_, 0) => (text, None),
        (n, used) => (&text[used..], Some(n)),
    }
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)
- Wrapper which implements the traits `crate::FromRadix10``crate::FromRadix10Checked``crate::FromRadix16``crate::FromRadix16Checked``One``Zero``+=`and`*=`.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRadix10.html)- Radix10
- Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 10
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRadix16.html)- Radix16
- Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 16
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRadix10Checked.html)- Radix10 - Checked
- Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 10.
Acts much like `FromRadix10`, but performs additional checks for overflows.
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRadix10Signed.html)- Radix10 - Signed
- Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 10. This
trait allows for an additional sign character (`+`or`-`) in front of the actual number in order, to allow for parsing negative values.
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRadix10SignedChecked.html)- Radix10 - Signed - Checked
- Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 10.
Acts much like `FromRadix10Signed`, but performs additional checks for overflows.
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRadix16Checked.html)- Radix16 - Checked
- Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 16.
Acts much like `FromRadix16`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [atoi](https://docs.rs/fn.atoi.html)
- Parses an integer from a slice.

## Expand description

A crate for parsing integers directly from ASCII (`[u8]`) without encoding them into utf8

# atoi 3.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/atoi/latest

# atoi-rs

Parse integers directly from `[u8]` slices in safe code

## Reasons to use this crate

Starting from a binary or ascii format you can parse an integer around three times as fast as with the more idiomatic detour over utf8. The crate comes with benchmarks so you can see for yourself.

The `FromRadix10Checked` trait also provides a way to parse integers very fast and safe, as its
implementation only performs checked arithmetics for the one digit that may actually overflow.

## Example

Parsing from a slice

```
use atoi;
assert_eq!;
```
Note that if you want to know how much of the input has been used, you can use the
`FromRadix10` trait, for example:

```
use FromRadix10;
/// Return the parsed integer and remaining slice if successful.
```
This [crate](https://www.crates.io/crates/atoi) has more to offer! Check out the full documentation
at [docs.rs](https://docs.rs/atoi).

---

# criterion - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/criterion/^0.8.2/

## Expand description

A statistics-driven micro-benchmarking library written in Rust.

This crate is a microbenchmarking library which aims to provide strong statistical confidence in detecting and estimating the size of performance improvements and regressions, while also being easy to use.

See
[the user guide](https://criterion-rs.github.io/book/index.html)
for examples as well as details on the measurement and analysis process,
and the output.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features:

- Collects detailed statistics, providing strong confidence that changes to performance are real, not measurement noise.
- Produces detailed charts, providing thorough understanding of your code’s performance behavior.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [async_](https://docs.rs/async_executor/index.html)- executor
- This module defines a trait that can be used to plug in different Futures executors into Criterion.rs’ async benchmarking support.
- [measurement](https://docs.rs/measurement/index.html)
- This module defines a set of traits that can be used to plug different measurements (eg.
Unix’s Processor Time, CPU or GPU performance counters, etc.) into Criterion.rs. It also
includes the `WallTime`
- [profiler](https://docs.rs/profiler/index.html)
- This module provides an extension trait which allows in-process profilers
to be hooked into the `--profile-time`argument at compile-time. Users of out-of-process profilers such as perf don’t need to do anything special.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [criterion_](https://docs.rs/macro.criterion_group.html)- group
- Macro used to define a function group for the benchmark harness; see the
`criterion_main!`
- [criterion_](https://docs.rs/macro.criterion_main.html)- main
- Macro which expands to a benchmark harness.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Async](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncBencher.html)- Bencher
- Async/await variant of `Bencher`
- [Bencher](https://docs.rs/struct.Bencher.html)
- Timer struct used to iterate a benchmarked function and measure the runtime.
- [Benchmark](https://docs.rs/struct.BenchmarkGroup.html)- Group
- Structure used to group together a set of related benchmarks, along with custom configuration settings for groups of benchmarks. All benchmarks performed using a benchmark group will be grouped together in the final report.
- [Benchmark](https://docs.rs/struct.BenchmarkId.html)- Id
- Simple structure representing an ID for a benchmark. The ID must be unique within a benchmark group.
- [Criterion](https://docs.rs/struct.Criterion.html)
- The benchmark manager
- [Plot](https://docs.rs/struct.PlotConfiguration.html)- Configuration
- Contains the configuration options for the plots generated by a particular benchmark or benchmark group.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Axis](https://docs.rs/enum.AxisScale.html)- Scale
- Axis scaling type. Specified via `PlotConfiguration::summary_scale`
- [Baseline](https://docs.rs/enum.Baseline.html)
- Baseline describes how the `baseline_directory`is handled.
- [Batch](https://docs.rs/enum.BatchSize.html)- Size
- Argument to `Bencher::iter_batched``Bencher::iter_batched_ref`
- [Benchmark](https://docs.rs/enum.BenchmarkFilter.html)- Filter
- Benchmark filtering support.
- [Plotting](https://docs.rs/enum.PlottingBackend.html)- Backend
- Enum used to select the plotting backend.
- [Sampling](https://docs.rs/enum.SamplingMode.html)- Mode
- This enum allows the user to control how Criterion.rs chooses the iteration count when sampling.
The default is `Auto`, which will choose a method automatically based on the iteration time during the warm-up phase.
- [Throughput](https://docs.rs/enum.Throughput.html)
- Enum representing different ways of measuring the throughput of benchmarked code. If the throughput setting is configured for a benchmark then the estimated throughput will be reported as well as the time per iteration.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [black_](https://docs.rs/fn.black_box.html)- box - Deprecated
- A function that is opaque to the optimizer, used to prevent the compiler from optimizing away computations in a benchmark.

# proptest - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/proptest/^1.4.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#proptest-reference-documentation)Proptest Reference Documentation

This is the reference documentation for the proptest API.

For documentation on how to get started with proptest and general usage
advice, please refer to the [Proptest Book](https://proptest-rs.github.io/proptest/intro.html).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [arbitrary](https://docs.rs/arbitrary/index.html)
- Defines the `Arbitrary`trait and related free functions and type aliases.
- [array](https://docs.rs/array/index.html)
- Support for strategies producing fixed-length arrays.
- [bits](https://docs.rs/bits/index.html)
- Strategies for working with bit sets.
- [bool](https://docs.rs/bool/index.html)
- Strategies for generating `bool`values.
- [char](https://docs.rs/char/index.html)
- Strategies for generating `char`values.
- [collection](https://docs.rs/collection/index.html)
- Strategies for generating `std::collections`of values.
- [num](https://docs.rs/num/index.html)
- Strategies to generate numeric values (as opposed to integers used as bit fields).
- [option](https://docs.rs/option/index.html)
- Strategies for generating `std::Option`values.
- [path](https://docs.rs/path/index.html)- `std`
- Strategies for generating [`PathBuf`] and related path types.
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Re-exports the most commonly-needed APIs of proptest.
- [range_](https://docs.rs/range_subset/index.html)- subset - `std`
- Strategies for generating values by taking samples of index ranges.
- [result](https://docs.rs/result/index.html)
- Strategies for combining delegate strategies into `std::Result`s.
- [sample](https://docs.rs/sample/index.html)
- Strategies for generating values by taking samples of collections.
- [strategy](https://docs.rs/strategy/index.html)
- Defines the core traits used by Proptest.
- [string](https://docs.rs/string/index.html)- `std`
- Strategies for generating strings and byte strings from regular expressions.
- [test_](https://docs.rs/test_runner/index.html)- runner
- State and functions for running proptest tests.
- [tuple](https://docs.rs/tuple/index.html)
- Support for combining strategies into tuples.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_assert.html)- assert
- Similar to `assert!`from std, but returns a test failure instead of panicking if the condition fails.
- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_assert_eq.html)- assert_ - eq
- Similar to `assert_eq!`from std, but returns a test failure instead of panicking if the condition fails.
- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_assert_ne.html)- assert_ - ne
- Similar to `assert_ne!`from std, but returns a test failure instead of panicking if the condition fails.
- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_assume.html)- assume
- Rejects the test input if assumptions are not met.
- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_compose.html)- compose
- Convenience to define functions which produce new strategies.
- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_oneof.html)- oneof
- Produce a strategy which picks one of the listed choices.
- [proptest](https://docs.rs/macro.proptest.html)
- Easily define `proptest`tests.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [property_](https://docs.rs/attr.property_test.html)- test - `attr-macro`
- The `property_test`procedural macro simplifies the creation of property-based tests using the`proptest`crate. This macro provides a more concise syntax for writing tests that automatically generate test cases based on properties.

# atoi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/atoi/latest/target-redirect/atoi/

## Expand description

A crate for parsing integers directly from ASCII (`[u8]`) without encoding them into utf8
first. The name is inspired by the famous C function.

Using `str::from_utf8` and `str::parse`
is likely to be more idiomatic. Use this crate if you want to avoid decoding bytes into utf8
(e.g. for performance reasons).

Note that if you want to know how much of the input has been used, you can use the
`FromRadix10` trait, for example:

```
use atoi::FromRadix10;
/// Return the parsed integer and remaining slice if successful.
fn atoi_with_rest<I: FromRadix10>(text: &[u8]) -> ((&[u8], Option<I>)) {
    match I::from_radix_10(text) {
        (_, 0) => (text, None),
        (n, used) => (&text[used..], Some(n)),
    }
}
```

- Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 10
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRadix16.html)- Radix16
- Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 16
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRadix10Checked.html)- Radix10 - Checked
- Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 10.
Acts much like `FromRadix10`, but performs additional checks for overflows.
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRadix10Signed.html)- Radix10 - Signed
- Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 10. This
trait allows for an additional sign character (`+`or`-`) in front of the actual number in order, to allow for parsing negative values.
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRadix10SignedChecked.html)- Radix10 - Signed - Checked
- Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 10.
Acts much like `FromRadix10Signed`, but performs additional checks for overflows.
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRadix16Checked.html)- Radix16 - Checked

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

§ Laws```

§ PurityThis function should return the same result at all times regardless of

# ordeal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal/0.3.0/ordeal/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#ordeal)Ordeal

`ordeal` (meaning “verdict / judgment”) is a specialized,
**certificate-checked** QF_BV SMT solver for the [PulseEngine](https://github.com/pulseengine) toolchain. It
exists to replace the Z3 static-link build pain that loom (verified WASM
optimizer) and synth (verified WASM→ARM codegen) carry today — grounding:
loom issue #246.

[§](https://docs.rs#design-in-one-paragraph)Design in one paragraph

An **untrusted solver** emits a machine-checkable **LRAT UNSAT
certificate**; a small **formally-verified checker** validates it. Only the
checker is trusted (the CompCert certifying-algorithm pattern; blueprint =
Lean 4 `bv_decide`, OOPSLA 2025). Z3 is demoted to a differential *oracle*
and benchmark *rival*, not the production engine. The pipeline is: term
graph → bit-blast → AIG → CNF (Tseitin) → SAT → LRAT → verified checker.

[§](https://docs.rs#modules)Modules

- `term`
- `solver`- `check-sat`interface and result types.
- `eval`
- `aig`
- `blast`
- `cnf`
- `sat`
- `lrat`- `ordeal-lrat`crate (the sole trusted component) validates it before any- `Unsat`is returned.
- [`oracle`] — the Z3 differential oracle (behind the`oracle`feature).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use solver::`- [Certificate](https://docs.rs/solver/struct.Certificate.html);
- `pub use solver::`- [CheckResult](https://docs.rs/solver/enum.CheckResult.html);
- `pub use solver::`- [Model](https://docs.rs/solver/struct.Model.html);
- `pub use solver::`- [Solver](https://docs.rs/solver/struct.Solver.html);
- `pub use term::`- [BoolTerm](https://docs.rs/term/enum.BoolTerm.html);
- `pub use term::`- [BvTerm](https://docs.rs/term/enum.BvTerm.html);
- `pub use term::`- [Sort](https://docs.rs/term/struct.Sort.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules-1)

- [aig](https://docs.rs/aig/index.html)
- And-Inverter Graph with structural hashing and constant folding (DES-002).
- [blast](https://docs.rs/blast/index.html)
- Bit-blasting rules: each QF_BV operation lowered to AIG gates (DES-005..DES-009), one module per op family.
- [cnf](https://docs.rs/cnf/index.html)
- CNF representation and the Tseitin encoder (DES-003).
- [eval](https://docs.rs/eval/index.html)
- Concrete evaluator for the closed QF_BV fragment — the executable SMT-LIB semantics (DES-001).
- [lrat](https://docs.rs/lrat/index.html)
- LRAT certificate emission from the CDCL proof trace (DES-013).
- [sat](https://docs.rs/sat/index.html)
- The pure-Rust CDCL SAT core (DES-004) — primary engine on every target.
- [sliver](https://docs.rs/sliver/index.html)
- The loom array/UF sliver (P3) — an extended query layer that is
**preprocessed away**into the closed QF_BV core before bit-blasting.
- [solver](https://docs.rs/solver/index.html)
- The one-shot solver interface and the P1 pipeline dispatcher (DES-012).
- [term](https://docs.rs/term/index.html)
- The `ordeal`term language: the closed QF_BV fragment from loom issue #246.

# ordeal_lrat - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal-lrat/0.3.0/ordeal_lrat/

## Expand description

Ordeal’s LRAT certificate checker — **the sole trusted component**.

The ordeal solver is untrusted: an `Unsat` answer is believed only when
this checker has validated an LRAT certificate for it. This crate is
written to be translated to Lean 4 (via Aeneas) and formally verified, so
everything here is deliberately small, simple, and obviously correct:
no `unsafe`, no dependencies, no cleverness.

[§](https://docs.rs#supported-dialect-textual-lrat-rup-only)Supported dialect: textual LRAT, **RUP-only**

**LOUD LIMITATION:** this checker supports only RUP (Reverse Unit
Propagation) addition steps. RAT steps — recognised by *negative* clause
ids in the hint list — are **rejected** with
[ CheckError::RatUnsupported](https://docs.rs/enum.CheckError.html#variant.RatUnsupported). This is deliberate: ordeal’s CDCL engine
emits RUP-only proofs, and rejecting is always sound (we may refuse a
valid certificate, we never accept an invalid one).

Accepted line forms (whitespace-separated integers, one step per line;
blank lines and lines starting with `c` are skipped as comments):

- Addition: `<id> <lit>* 0 <hint>* 0`— adds the clause`<lit>*`with id`<id>`, justified by unit propagation through the clauses named by`<hint>*`, in order.
- Deletion: `<id> d <id>* 0`— marks the named clauses dead. The leading`<id>`is informational (as emitted by drat-trim) and is not checked.

Clause ids are 1-based: original clause `i` of the input CNF (0-based)
has id `i + 1`; each addition step must then use exactly the next
sequential id (this is what ordeal emits; sparse ids are rejected).

[§](https://docs.rs#what-checked-means)What “checked” means

An addition step `C` with hints `h1..hk` is verified by assuming the
negation of every literal of `C` and then unit-propagating through the
hint clauses in order: each hint must be either *falsified* (conflict —
the step is verified, so CNF ∧ ¬C is unsat, i.e. CNF ⊨ C) or *unit*
(its single unassigned literal is assigned true). Anything else —
a satisfied hint, a hint with two or more unassigned literals, running
out of hints, a dead or unknown id — rejects the certificate.

The whole certificate is accepted iff it parses in full AND some verified
addition step adds the **empty clause** (checking stops at that step;
parsed trailing steps are ignored). Parsing everything first is stricter
than strictly necessary and always sound (extra rejections only).

[§](https://docs.rs#structure-parser-vs-kernel)Structure: parser vs kernel

The crate is split for the formal proof (issue #12): the [ kernel](https://docs.rs/kernel/index.html)
module is the string-free checking core — the Aeneas → Lean translation
target carrying the soundness theorem — and this file is the untrusted
text parser feeding it. The CNF reaches the kernel directly, so parser
bugs cannot manufacture an acceptance (see

`kernel` docs).## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [kernel](https://docs.rs/kernel/index.html)
- The string-free checking core — **the Aeneas → Lean translation target**.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Check](https://docs.rs/enum.CheckError.html)- Error
- Why a certificate was rejected (or could not even be read).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [check](https://docs.rs/fn.check.html)
- Check a textual LRAT `certificate`against the input`cnf`.

# tenuo - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tenuo/0.2.3/tenuo/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#tenuo-core)Tenuo Core

Agent Capability Flow Control - Rust core library.

Tenuo provides cryptographically-enforced capability attenuation for AI agent workflows. Unlike traditional IAM systems that answer “Who are you?”, Tenuo answers “Who delegated this authority, what task context does it carry, and is this action within the delegated bounds?”

[§](https://docs.rs#key-concepts)Key Concepts

- **Warrant**: A transferable token of authority containing tool name, constraints, TTL, and signature
- **Attenuation**: Capabilities can only shrink when delegated, never expand
- **Constraints**: Restrictions on argument values (Pattern, Exact, OneOf, Range, CEL)

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use tenuo::{Warrant, Pattern, Keypair};
use std::time::Duration;
// Create a keypair for the control plane
let keypair = SigningKey::generate();
// Issue a warrant for cluster upgrades
let warrant = Warrant::builder()
    .capability("upgrade_cluster")
    .constraint("cluster", Pattern::new("staging-*"))
    .ttl(Duration::from_secs(600))
    .build(&keypair)?;
// Attenuate to a narrower scope for a worker agent
let worker_warrant = warrant.attenuate()
    .constraint("cluster", Exact::new("staging-web"))
    .build(&worker_keypair)?;
```

# harn_rules - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/harn-rules/0.8.168/harn_rules/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#harn-rules)harn-rules

The declarative structural rule engine for Harn — the Rust core that
powers `harn rules` / lint / codemod surfaces. A **rule** describes
*what to match* (a pattern snippet, a node kind, or a regex) and
optionally *how to rewrite* it (a `fix`); the engine compiles that rule
against the tree-sitter machinery in [ harn_hostlib::ast](https://docs.rs/harn-hostlib/0.8.168/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/harn_hostlib/ast/index.html) and produces

[es with metavariable bindings.](https://docs.rs/engine/struct.RuleMatch.html)

`RuleMatch`This crate delivers the **atomic matching tier** (#2832), the
**relational + composite algebra** (#2833), the **predicate + rewrite
layer** (#2834), and the **safety + idempotency gate** (#2835):

- `model`- `RuleNode`- `pattern`/- `kind`/- `regex`, relational- `inside`/- `has`/- `follows`/- `precedes`, composite- `all`/- `any`/- `not`/- `matches`) plus- `where`/- `transform`/- `fix`and- `utils`.
- `pattern`- `$VAR`metavariable lifting, unification, literal patterns, and typed- `$VAR:kind`placeholders).
- `evaluator`- utility-rule reuse).

- `constraint`- `where`predicates on captured metavars (regex, comparison, recursive sub-pattern, and Harn-only semantic filters).
- `transform`- `replace`/- `substring`/- `convert`) before fixing.
- `fix`- `fix`template interpolation and format-preserving splice.
- `engine`- `Rule`- `CompiledRule::apply`- `CompiledRule::auto_apply`- `CompiledRule::apply_checked`- `Diagnostic`
- `recipe`- `ScanningRecipe`- `run_recipe`
- `report`- `DataTable`
- `loader`
- semantic capture metadata — Harn captures gain resolved binding identity and simple static type labels when the local syntax provides them.

The whole-project scan lifecycle (#2836) layers onto this surface.

```
use harn_rules::{Rule, CompiledRule};
let rule = Rule::from_toml_str(
    r#"
    id = "destructure-default"
    language = "typescript"
    fix = "{ $KEY: $SRC }"
    [rule]
    pattern = "$SRC?.$KEY ?? $DEFAULT"
    "#,
).unwrap();
let compiled = CompiledRule::compile(&rule).unwrap();
let matches = compiled.run("const a = cfg?.timeout ?? 30;").unwrap();
assert_eq!(matches[0].bindings["KEY"].text, "timeout");
```

# harn_lint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/harn-lint/0.8.168/harn_lint/

## Expand description

Harn’s lint crate. The public surface is intentionally narrow: a
handful of `lint_*` entry points, the diagnostic and options types,
and a couple of small utility functions reused by other crates. All
walk state, rule dispatch, and source-aware rule implementations
live in sibling modules.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [native](https://docs.rs/native/index.html)
- C-compatible ABI for native lint rule libraries.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Lint](https://docs.rs/struct.LintDiagnostic.html)- Diagnostic
- A lint diagnostic reported by the linter.
- [Lint](https://docs.rs/struct.LintOptions.html)- Options
- Extra options for source-aware lint rules (path-aware rules, opt-in
rules like `require-file-header`).

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Lint](https://docs.rs/enum.LintSeverity.html)- Severity
- Severity level for lint diagnostics.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_COMPLEXITY_THRESHOLD.html)- COMPLEXITY_ - THRESHOLD
- Default cyclomatic-complexity threshold. Callers can override via
`LintOptions::complexity_threshold``[lint].complexity_threshold`in`harn.toml`). Chosen to match Clippy’s`cognitive_complexity`default and sit between ESLint (20) and gocyclo (30); Harn’s scorer counts`&&`/`||`per operator, so real-world Harn functions score a notch higher than in tools that only count control-flow nodes.
- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_TEMPLATE_VARIANT_BRANCH_THRESHOLD.html)- TEMPLATE_ - VARIANT_ - BRANCH_ - THRESHOLD
- Default threshold; see [`template_variant_branch_threshold`] in`harn_cli::config::LintConfig`. Picked to match the issue’s stated default (#1669).
- [GENERATED_](https://docs.rs/constant.GENERATED_HARN_SUFFIX.html)- HARN_ - SUFFIX
- The filename suffix that marks a machine-generated Harn source file:
`<name>.generated.harn`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [collect_](https://docs.rs/fn.collect_selective_import_names.html)- selective_ - import_ - names
- Extract all function names that appear in selective import statements
(`import { foo, bar } from "module"`).
- [derive_](https://docs.rs/fn.derive_file_header_title.html)- file_ - header_ - title
- Derive the title shown inside the autofix’s file-header block. Falls back to a generic “Module.” when no path is available. Only the first letter is capitalized — not every word — per the header style.
- [is_](https://docs.rs/fn.is_generated_path.html)- generated_ - path
- True if `path`names a machine-generated Harn file (`*.generated.harn`).
- [lint](https://docs.rs/fn.lint.html)
- Lint an AST program and return all diagnostics.
- [lint_](https://docs.rs/fn.lint_diagnostics_from_type_diagnostics.html)- diagnostics_ - from_ - type_ - diagnostics
- Convert type-checker diagnostics tagged as lint rules into ordinary lint diagnostics so CLI/editor callers can share rule filtering, rendering, and autofix plumbing.
- [lint_](https://docs.rs/fn.lint_prompt_template.html)- prompt_ - template
- Lint a single `.harn.prompt`template source. Returns the diagnostics produced by the template-specific lint rules (`template-provider-identity-branch`,`template-variant-explosion`).
- [lint_](https://docs.rs/fn.lint_with_config.html)- with_ - config
- Lint an AST program, filtering out diagnostics for disabled rules.
- [lint_](https://docs.rs/fn.lint_with_config_and_source.html)- with_ - config_ - and_ - source
- Lint an AST program, optionally using the original source for source-aware rules.
- [lint_](https://docs.rs/fn.lint_with_cross_file_imports.html)- with_ - cross_ - file_ - imports
- Lint with cross-file import awareness. Functions named in
`externally_imported_names`are exempt from the unused-function lint even without local references.
- [lint_](https://docs.rs/fn.lint_with_module_graph.html)- with_ - module_ - graph
- Lint with cross-file import awareness driven by `harn_modules::ModuleGraph`
- [lint_](https://docs.rs/fn.lint_with_options.html)- with_ - options
- Lint with cross-file import awareness plus extra `LintOptions`
- [lint_](https://docs.rs/fn.lint_with_source.html)- with_ - source
- Lint an AST program with source-aware rules enabled.
- [simplify_](https://docs.rs/fn.simplify_bool_comparison.html)- bool_ - comparison
- Simplify a boolean comparison expression like `x == true`→`x`.
- [type_](https://docs.rs/fn.type_diagnostic_lint_disabled.html)- diagnostic_ - lint_ - disabled
- Returns true when a type diagnostic is a lint diagnostic disabled by the caller’s lint configuration.

# harn_hostlib - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/harn-hostlib/0.8.168/harn_hostlib/

## Expand description

`harn-hostlib`: opt-in host builtins for code intelligence (tree-sitter,
repo scanning, deterministic indexing) and tool execution (search, file
I/O, git, process lifecycle, file watcher).

This crate is the Rust home of two classes of optional host capabilities:

- **Code intelligence**—- `ast/`,- `code_index/`,- `scanner/`,- `fs_watch/`.
- **Deterministic tools**—- `tools/`(search, fs, git, process).

These don’t belong inside `harn-vm` — pulling tree-sitter grammars,
ripgrep, and `notify` into the VM would balloon the footprint of every
pipeline that doesn’t index host code. Instead, this crate exposes a
single [ HostlibCapability](https://docs.rs/trait.HostlibCapability.html) trait. Embedders such as

`harn-cli`’s ACP
server) compose the modules they need via [and wire the resulting builtins into the VM through](https://docs.rs/struct.HostlibRegistry.html)

`HostlibRegistry`[/](https://docs.rs/harn-vm/0.8.168/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/harn_vm/vm/state/struct.Vm.html#method.register_builtin)

`harn_vm::Vm::register_builtin`[.](https://docs.rs/harn-vm/0.8.168/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/harn_vm/vm/state/struct.Vm.html#method.register_async_builtin)

`harn_vm::Vm::register_async_builtin`[§](https://docs.rs#status)Status

The AST, scanner, code-index, and deterministic-tool surfaces are
implemented. `fs_watch/` still registers its public contract with
[ HostlibError::Unimplemented](https://docs.rs/error/enum.HostlibError.html#variant.Unimplemented) handlers. Module names, method names,
and JSON schemas under

`schemas/` are the source of truth for hostlib
request/response compatibility, so they must stay stable while module
bodies evolve.## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use error::`- [HostlibError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.HostlibError.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [ast](https://docs.rs/ast/index.html)
- AST host capability.
- [code_](https://docs.rs/code_index/index.html)- index
- Code index host capability.
- [embed](https://docs.rs/embed/index.html)
- Text-similarity / embedding host capability.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Error type for hostlib host calls.
- [fs](https://docs.rs/fs/index.html)
- Session-scoped staged filesystem mode.
- [fs_](https://docs.rs/fs_snapshot/index.html)- snapshot
- Per-tool-call filesystem snapshots — Gemini-style `/restore`primitives.
- [fs_](https://docs.rs/fs_watch/index.html)- watch
- File-system watch host capability.
- [host_](https://docs.rs/host_env_custody/index.html)- env_ - custody
- Shared host-environment custody contracts.
- [process](https://docs.rs/process/index.html)
- Process abstraction used by the deterministic process tools.
- [sandbox](https://docs.rs/sandbox/index.html)
- The runtime arm of the permission primitive: pluggable sandbox
backends that *enforce*a declared policy rather than merely gating tool dispatch.
- [scanner](https://docs.rs/scanner/index.html)
- Repo scanner host capability.
- [schemas](https://docs.rs/schemas/index.html)
- Embedded JSON Schemas for every hostlib host method.
- [secret_](https://docs.rs/secret_store/index.html)- store
- Per-OS secret-store host primitive.
- [tools](https://docs.rs/tools/index.html)
- Deterministic tools capability.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Builtin](https://docs.rs/struct.BuiltinRegistry.html)- Registry
- Mutable collector each capability writes into during `register`.
- [Hostlib](https://docs.rs/struct.HostlibRegistry.html)- Registry
- Composes capabilities and emits VM registrations.
- [Registered](https://docs.rs/struct.RegisteredBuiltin.html)- Builtin
- One registered builtin. The name is what Harn scripts call (e.g.
`hostlib_ast_parse_file`);`module`and`method`are the canonical schema-directory coordinates (`schemas/<module>/<method>.request.json`).

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Hostlib](https://docs.rs/trait.HostlibCapability.html)- Capability
- One module’s worth of builtins. Kept tiny on purpose: capabilities exist purely so tests can reason about the surface without booting a VM, and so embedders can opt into individual modules.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [install_](https://docs.rs/fn.install_default.html)- default
- Convenience: build a `HostlibRegistry`populated with every capability the crate ships, register them on the supplied VM, and return the registry so callers can introspect (e.g. for schema-drift tests).

# harn_serve - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/harn-serve/0.8.168/harn_serve/

Rate-limiting + backpressure + call-budget primitive for .harn
handlers hosted on harn-serve. Implements epic A.11 — the
cross-tenant production-readiness shape a cloud gateway enforces
today via bespoke middleware (http_utils::check_rate_limits), lifted
into one declarative primitive every adapter on harn-serve shares.

Wires harn-serve::AuthPolicy into the supervised MCP host
primitive (harn_vm::mcp_host) without making harn-vm depend on
harn-serve. The pattern matches the connector-client / observability
installers elsewhere in the workspace: harn-vm exposes a pluggable
callback; harn-serve installs an adapter at boot time.

A single API key paired with the scopes the key grants. Two keys
pointing at the same secret with different scope sets are treated as
separate entries; the first match wins.

RAII guard returned by enter_auth_context. Popping the stack on
drop keeps the ambient scope balanced even when the dispatched
callable panics or returns an error.

Tenant-scoped allowlist for the harness.mcp.* host primitive.
Each entry maps an MCP server name to the tools that tenant is
allowed to invoke on it. An entry whose tool set is All allows
every tool the server advertises; an explicit Only(...) set
restricts callers to the named tools (case-sensitive match against
the server-advertised tool name).

Declarative route auth-policy metadata declared via @policy(...),
composing with the @scopes requirement rather than replacing it.
allowed_kinds is enforced by the harn serve site admission layer;
match_labels and method_guards are exported for audit tooling that
needs to confirm a handler declares resource/tenant/JSON-RPC method
guards implemented by std/harness/policy.require_policy(...).

An HTTP method + path a .harn handler answers under harn serve site. Declared with @route("GET", "/users/{id}") or inferred from
the handler_* naming convention.

Stable ACP methodId for harn’s local “no credential required”
flow. Advertised when an AuthPolicy has no configured methods so
the initialize handshake stays spec conformant (a non-empty
authMethods array). Authenticating against this id is a no-op:
callers are already accepted as anonymous.

Default 10 MiB body size cap applied to every HTTP router exposed by
the harn-serve adapters (MCP, A2A, API). Matches the orchestrator
listener’s DEFAULT_MAX_BODY_BYTES so large/malicious POSTs cannot
exhaust process memory while axum buffers the request before
handing it to a handler.

Print catalog diagnostics to stderr at server startup, matching the
[harn] … banner the adapters already emit. Standalone serve
commands call this so authors see malformed attributes immediately;
embedders that build a router directly can read
ExportCatalog::diagnostics and render them in their own UI.

Structured forbidden payload shared across adapter error envelopes
(MCP JSON-RPC error.data, A2A JSON-RPC error.data, REST error
body). Producing it from one place keeps the field layout
(kind/required_scopes/granted_scopes/missing_scopes) stable
for clients that parse it programmatically.

Render a stable diagnostic for a scope-mismatch decision. Used both
by DispatchError::Forbidden::message() and by adapter-layer error
envelopes (JSON-RPC data.message, HTTP body, ACP error reply) so
callers see the same text everywhere.

---

# atoi 3.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/atoi/3.1.0

# atoi-rs

Parse integers directly from `[u8]` slices in safe code

## Reasons to use this crate

Starting from a binary or ascii format you can parse an integer around three times as fast as with the more idiomatic detour over utf8. The crate comes with benchmarks so you can see for yourself.

The `FromRadix10Checked` trait also provides a way to parse integers very fast and safe, as its
implementation only performs checked arithmetics for the one digit that may actually overflow.

## Example

Parsing from a slice

```
use atoi;
assert_eq!;
```
Note that if you want to know how much of the input has been used, you can use the
`FromRadix10` trait, for example:

```
use FromRadix10;
/// Return the parsed integer and remaining slice if successful.
```
This [crate](https://www.crates.io/crates/atoi) has more to offer! Check out the full documentation
at [docs.rs](https://docs.rs/atoi).

---

# atoi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/atoi/3.1.0/target-redirect/atoi/

## Expand description

A crate for parsing integers directly from ASCII (`[u8]`) without encoding them into utf8
first. The name is inspired by the famous C function.

Using `str::from_utf8` and `str::parse`
is likely to be more idiomatic. Use this crate if you want to avoid decoding bytes into utf8
(e.g. for performance reasons).

Note that if you want to know how much of the input has been used, you can use the
`FromRadix10` trait, for example:

```
use atoi::FromRadix10;
/// Return the parsed integer and remaining slice if successful.
fn atoi_with_rest<I: FromRadix10>(text: &[u8]) -> ((&[u8], Option<I>)) {
    match I::from_radix_10(text) {
        (_, 0) => (text, None),
        (n, used) => (&text[used..], Some(n)),
    }
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)
- Wrapper which implements the traits `crate::FromRadix10``crate::FromRadix10Checked``crate::FromRadix16``crate::FromRadix16Checked``One``Zero``+=`and`*=`.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRadix10.html)- Radix10
- Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 10
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRadix16.html)- Radix16
- Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 16
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRadix10Checked.html)- Radix10 - Checked
- Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 10.
Acts much like `FromRadix10`, but performs additional checks for overflows.
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRadix10Signed.html)- Radix10 - Signed
- Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 10. This
trait allows for an additional sign character (`+`or`-`) in front of the actual number in order, to allow for parsing negative values.
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRadix10SignedChecked.html)- Radix10 - Signed - Checked
- Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 10.
Acts much like `FromRadix10Signed`, but performs additional checks for overflows.
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRadix16Checked.html)- Radix16 - Checked
- Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 16.
Acts much like `FromRadix16`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [atoi](https://docs.rs/fn.atoi.html)
- Parses an integer from a slice.

# atoi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/atoi/3.1.0/atoi/index.html

## Expand description

A crate for parsing integers directly from ASCII (`[u8]`) without encoding them into utf8
first. The name is inspired by the famous C function.

Using `str::from_utf8` and `str::parse`
is likely to be more idiomatic. Use this crate if you want to avoid decoding bytes into utf8
(e.g. for performance reasons).

Note that if you want to know how much of the input has been used, you can use the
`FromRadix10` trait, for example:

```
use atoi::FromRadix10;
/// Return the parsed integer and remaining slice if successful.
fn atoi_with_rest<I: FromRadix10>(text: &[u8]) -> ((&[u8], Option<I>)) {
    match I::from_radix_10(text) {
        (_, 0) => (text, None),
        (n, used) => (&text[used..], Some(n)),
    }
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Integer](https://docs.rs/struct.Integer.html)
- Wrapper which implements the traits `crate::FromRadix10``crate::FromRadix10Checked``crate::FromRadix16``crate::FromRadix16Checked``One``Zero``+=`and`*=`.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRadix10.html)- Radix10
- Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 10
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRadix16.html)- Radix16
- Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 16
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRadix10Checked.html)- Radix10 - Checked
- Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 10.
Acts much like `FromRadix10`, but performs additional checks for overflows.
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRadix10Signed.html)- Radix10 - Signed
- Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 10. This
trait allows for an additional sign character (`+`or`-`) in front of the actual number in order, to allow for parsing negative values.
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRadix10SignedChecked.html)- Radix10 - Signed - Checked
- Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 10.

# atoi/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! A crate for parsing integers directly from ASCII (`[u8]`) without encoding them into utf8
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//! first. The name is inspired by the famous C function.
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//!
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! Using `str::from_utf8` and `str::parse`
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! is likely to be more idiomatic. Use this crate if you want to avoid decoding bytes into utf8
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! (e.g. for performance reasons).
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//!
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! Note that if you want to know how much of the input has been used, you can use the
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! `FromRadix10` trait, for example:
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! ```rust
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! use atoi::FromRadix10;
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! /// Return the parsed integer and remaining slice if successful.
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! fn atoi_with_rest<I: FromRadix10>(text: &[u8]) -> ((&[u8], Option<I>)) {
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!     match I::from_radix_10(text) {
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//!         (_, 0) => (text, None),
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!         (n, used) => (&text[used..], Some(n)),
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!     }
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! }
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! ```
[22](https://docs.rs#22)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "std"), no_std)]
[23](https://docs.rs#23)
[24](https://docs.rs#24)mod builtin;
[25](https://docs.rs#25)mod integer;
[26](https://docs.rs#26)
[27](https://docs.rs#27)pub use integer::Integer;
[28](https://docs.rs#28)
[29](https://docs.rs#29)/// Parses an integer from a slice.
[30](https://docs.rs#30)///
[31](https://docs.rs#31)/// Contrary to its 'C' counterpart atoi is generic and will require a type argument if the type
[32](https://docs.rs#32)/// inference can not determine its result. It will also check for overflow / underflow and allow
[33](https://docs.rs#33)/// for Signs.
[34](https://docs.rs#34)///
[35](https://docs.rs#35)/// Use [`FromRadix10`] or [`FromRadix10Checked`] directly if you do not want to allow signs. Use
[36](https://docs.rs#36)/// [`FromRadix10`] or [`FromRadix10Signed`] if you want to opt out overflow / underflow checking.
[37](https://docs.rs#37)///
[38](https://docs.rs#38)/// # Example
[39](https://docs.rs#39)///
[40](https://docs.rs#40)/// ```
[41](https://docs.rs#41)/// use atoi::atoi;
[42](https://docs.rs#42)/// // Parsing to digits from a slice
[43](https://docs.rs#43)/// assert_eq!(Some(42), atoi::<u32>(b"42"));
[44](https://docs.rs#44)/// // Additional bytes after the number are ignored. If you want to know how many bytes were used
[45](https://docs.rs#45)/// // to parse the number use `FromRadix10::from_radix_10`.
[46](https://docs.rs#46)/// assert_eq!(Some(42), atoi::<u32>(b"42 is the answer to life, the universe and everything"));
[47](https://docs.rs#47)/// // `None` is returned if the slice does not start with a digit
[48](https://docs.rs#48)/// assert_eq!(None, atoi::<u32>(b"Sadly we do not know the question"));
[49](https://docs.rs#49)/// // While signed integer types are supported...
[50](https://docs.rs#50)/// assert_eq!(Some(42), atoi::<i32>(b"42"));
[51](https://docs.rs#51)/// // Signs are allowed.
[52](https://docs.rs#52)/// assert_eq!(Some(-42), atoi::<i32>(b"-42"));
[53](https://docs.rs#53)/// // Leading zeros are allowed
[54](https://docs.rs#54)/// assert_eq!(Some(42), atoi::<u32>(b"0042"));
[55](https://docs.rs#55)/// // Overflows will return `None`
[56](https://docs.rs#56)/// assert_eq!(None, atoi::<u8>(b"256"));
[57](https://docs.rs#57)/// ```
[58](https://docs.rs#58)///
[59](https://docs.rs#59)/// # Return
[60](https://docs.rs#60)///
[61](https://docs.rs#61)/// Returns a a number if the slice started with a number, otherwise `None` is returned.
[62](https://docs.rs#62)#[inline]
[63](https://docs.rs#63)pub fn atoi<I>(text: &[u8]) -> Option<I>
[64](https://docs.rs#64)where
[65](https://docs.rs#65)    I: FromRadix10SignedChecked,
[66](https://docs.rs#66){
[67](https://docs.rs#67)    match I::from_radix_10_signed_checked(text) {
[68](https://docs.rs#68)        (_, 0) | (None, _) => None,
[69](https://docs.rs#69)        (Some(n), _) => Some(n),
[70](https://docs.rs#70)    }
[71](https://docs.rs#71)}
[72](https://docs.rs#72)
[73](https://docs.rs#73)/// Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 10
[74](https://docs.rs#74)pub trait FromRadix10: Sized {
[75](https://docs.rs#75)    /// Parses an integer from a slice.
[76](https://docs.rs#76)    ///
[77](https://docs.rs#77)    /// # Example
[78](https://docs.rs#78)    ///
[79](https://docs.rs#79)    /// ```
[80](https://docs.rs#80)    /// use atoi::FromRadix10;
[81](https://docs.rs#81)    /// // Parsing to digits from a slice
[82](https://docs.rs#82)    /// assert_eq!((42,2), u32::from_radix_10(b"42"));
[83](https://docs.rs#83)    /// // Additional bytes after the number are ignored
[84](https://docs.rs#84)    /// assert_eq!((42,2), u32::from_radix_10(b"42 is the answer to life, the universe and everything"));
[85](https://docs.rs#85)    /// // (0,0) is returned if the slice does not start with a digit
[86](https://docs.rs#86)    /// assert_eq!((0,0), u32::from_radix_10(b"Sadly we do not know the question"));
[87](https://docs.rs#87)    /// // While signed integer types are supported...
[88](https://docs.rs#88)    /// assert_eq!((42,2), i32::from_radix_10(b"42"));
[89](https://docs.rs#89)    /// // Signs are not allowed (even for signed integer types)
[90](https://docs.rs#90)    /// assert_eq!((0,0), i32::from_radix_10(b"-42"));
[91](https://docs.rs#91)    /// // Leading zeros are allowed
[92](https://docs.rs#92)    /// assert_eq!((42,4), u32::from_radix_10(b"0042"));
[93](https://docs.rs#93)    /// ```
[94](https://docs.rs#94)    ///
[95](https://docs.rs#95)    /// # Return
[96](https://docs.rs#96)    ///
[97](https://docs.rs#97)    /// Returns a tuple with two numbers. The first is the integer parsed or zero, the second is the
[98](https://docs.rs#98)    /// index of the byte right after the parsed number. If the second element is zero the slice
[99](https://docs.rs#99)    /// did not start with an ASCII digit.
[100](https://docs.rs#100)    fn from_radix_10(_: &[u8]) -> (Self, usize);
[101](https://docs.rs#101)}
[102](https://docs.rs#102)
[103](https://docs.rs#103)/// Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 10.
[104](https://docs.rs#104)/// Acts much like `FromRadix10`, but performs additional checks for overflows.
[105](https://docs.rs#105)pub trait FromRadix10Checked: Sized {
[106](https://docs.rs#106)    /// Parses an integer from a slice.
[107](https://docs.rs#107)    ///
[108](https://docs.rs#108)    /// # Example
[109](https://docs.rs#109)    ///
[110](https://docs.rs#110)    /// ```
[111](https://docs.rs#111)    /// use atoi::FromRadix10Checked;
[112](https://docs.rs#112)    /// // Parsing to digits from a slice
[113](https://docs.rs#113)    /// assert_eq!((Some(42),2), u32::from_radix_10_checked(b"42"));
[114](https://docs.rs#114)    /// // Additional bytes after the number are ignored
[115](https://docs.rs#115)    /// assert_eq!((Some(42),2), u32::from_radix_10_checked(b"42 is the answer to life, the universe and everything"));
[116](https://docs.rs#116)    /// // (0,0) is returned if the slice does not start with a digit
[117](https://docs.rs#117)    /// assert_eq!((Some(0),0), u32::from_radix_10_checked(b"Sadly we do not know the question"));
[118](https://docs.rs#118)    /// // While signed integer types are supported...
[119](https://docs.rs#119)    /// assert_eq!((Some(42),2), i32::from_radix_10_checked(b"42"));
[120](https://docs.rs#120)    /// // Signs are not allowed (even for signed integer types)
[121](https://docs.rs#121)    /// assert_eq!((Some(0),0), i32::from_radix_10_checked(b"-42"));
[122](https://docs.rs#122)    /// // Leading zeros are allowed
[123](https://docs.rs#123)    /// assert_eq!((Some(42),4), u32::from_radix_10_checked(b"0042"));
[124](https://docs.rs#124)    /// // Overflow is indicated by `None`
[125](https://docs.rs#125)    /// assert_eq!((None, 3), u8::from_radix_10_checked(b"256"));
[126](https://docs.rs#126)    /// ```
[127](https://docs.rs#127)    ///
[128](https://docs.rs#128)    /// # Return
[129](https://docs.rs#129)    ///
[130](https://docs.rs#130)    /// Returns a tuple with two numbers. The first is the integer parsed or zero if no digit has
[131](https://docs.rs#131)    /// been found. None, if there were too many, or too high dighits and the parsing overflowed.
[132](https://docs.rs#132)    /// The second is the index of the byte right after the parsed number. If the second element is
[133](https://docs.rs#133)    /// zero the slice did not start with an ASCII digit.
[134](https://docs.rs#134)    fn from_radix_10_checked(_: &[u8]) -> (Option<Self>, usize);
[135](https://docs.rs#135)}
[136](https://docs.rs#136)
[137](https://docs.rs#137)/// Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 16
[138](https://docs.rs#138)pub trait FromRadix16: Sized {
[139](https://docs.rs#139)    /// Parses an integer from a slice.
[140](https://docs.rs#140)    ///
[141](https://docs.rs#141)    /// # Example
[142](https://docs.rs#142)    ///
[143](https://docs.rs#143)    /// ```
[144](https://docs.rs#144)    /// use atoi::FromRadix16;
[145](https://docs.rs#145)    /// // Parsing to digits from a slice
[146](https://docs.rs#146)    /// assert_eq!((42,2), u32::from_radix_16(b"2a"));
[147](https://docs.rs#147)    /// // Additional bytes after the number are ignored
[148](https://docs.rs#148)    /// assert_eq!((42,2), u32::from_radix_16(b"2a is the answer to life, the universe and everything"));
[149](https://docs.rs#149)    /// // (0,0) is returned if the slice does not start with a digit
[150](https://docs.rs#150)    /// assert_eq!((0,0), u32::from_radix_16(b"Sadly we do not know the question"));
[151](https://docs.rs#151)    /// // While signed integer types are supported...
[152](https://docs.rs#152)    /// assert_eq!((42,2), i32::from_radix_16(b"2a"));
[153](https://docs.rs#153)    /// // Signs are not allowed (even for signed integer types)
[154](https://docs.rs#154)    /// assert_eq!((0,0), i32::from_radix_16(b"-2a"));
[155](https://docs.rs#155)    /// // Leading zeros are allowed
[156](https://docs.rs#156)    /// assert_eq!((42,4), u32::from_radix_16(b"002a"));
[157](https://docs.rs#157)    /// // so are uppercase letters
[158](https://docs.rs#158)    /// assert_eq!((42,4), u32::from_radix_16(b"002A"));
[159](https://docs.rs#159)    /// ```
[160](https://docs.rs#160)    ///
[161](https://docs.rs#161)    /// # Return
[162](https://docs.rs#162)    ///
[163](https://docs.rs#163)    /// Returns a tuple with two numbers. The first is the integer parsed or zero, the second is the
[164](https://docs.rs#164)    /// index of the byte right after the parsed number. If the second element is zero the slice
[165](https://docs.rs#165)    /// did not start with an ASCII digit.
[166](https://docs.rs#166)    fn from_radix_16(_: &[u8]) -> (Self, usize);
[167](https://docs.rs#167)}
[168](https://docs.rs#168)
[169](https://docs.rs#169)/// Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 16.
[170](https://docs.rs#170)/// Acts much like [`FromRadix16`], but performs additional checks for overflows.
[171](https://docs.rs#171)pub trait FromRadix16Checked: Sized {
[172](https://docs.rs#172)    /// Parses an integer from a slice.
[173](https://docs.rs#173)    ///
[174](https://docs.rs#174)    /// # Example
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    ///
[176](https://docs.rs#176)    /// ```
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    /// use atoi::FromRadix16Checked;
[178](https://docs.rs#178)    /// // Parsing to digits from a slice
[179](https://docs.rs#179)    /// assert_eq!((Some(42),2), u32::from_radix_16_checked(b"2a"));
[180](https://docs.rs#180)    /// // Additional bytes after the number are ignored
[181](https://docs.rs#181)    /// assert_eq!((Some(42),2), u32::from_radix_16_checked(b"2a is the answer to life, the \
[182](https://docs.rs#182)    /// universe and everything"));
[183](https://docs.rs#183)    /// // (0,0) is returned if the slice does not start with a digit
[184](https://docs.rs#184)    /// assert_eq!((Some(0),0), u32::from_radix_16_checked(b"Sadly we do not know the question"));
[185](https://docs.rs#185)    /// // While signed integer types are supported...
[186](https://docs.rs#186)    /// assert_eq!((Some(42),2), i32::from_radix_16_checked(b"2a"));
[187](https://docs.rs#187)    /// // Signs are not allowed (even for signed integer types)
[188](https://docs.rs#188)    /// assert_eq!((Some(0),0), i32::from_radix_16_checked(b"-2a"));
[189](https://docs.rs#189)    /// // Leading zeros are allowed
[190](https://docs.rs#190)    /// assert_eq!((Some(42),4), u32::from_radix_16_checked(b"002a"));
[191](https://docs.rs#191)    /// // So are uppercase letters
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    /// assert_eq!((Some(42),2), u32::from_radix_16_checked(b"2A"))
[193](https://docs.rs#193)    /// ```
[194](https://docs.rs#194)    ///
[195](https://docs.rs#195)    /// # Return
[196](https://docs.rs#196)    ///
[197](https://docs.rs#197)    /// Returns a tuple with two numbers. The first is the integer parsed or zero if no digit has
[198](https://docs.rs#198)    /// been found. None, if there were too many, or too high dighits and the parsing overflowed.
[199](https://docs.rs#199)    /// The second is the index of the byte right after the parsed number. If the second element is
[200](https://docs.rs#200)    /// zero the slice did not start with an ASCII digit.
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    fn from_radix_16_checked(_: &[u8]) -> (Option<Self>, usize);
[202](https://docs.rs#202)}
[203](https://docs.rs#203)
[204](https://docs.rs#204)/// Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 10. This
[205](https://docs.rs#205)/// trait allows for an additional sign character (`+` or `-`) in front of the actual number in
[206](https://docs.rs#206)/// order, to allow for parsing negative values.
[207](https://docs.rs#207)pub trait FromRadix10Signed: Sized {
[208](https://docs.rs#208)    /// Parses an integer from a slice.
[209](https://docs.rs#209)    ///
[210](https://docs.rs#210)    /// # Example
[211](https://docs.rs#211)    ///
[212](https://docs.rs#212)    /// ```
[213](https://docs.rs#213)    /// use atoi::FromRadix10Signed;
[214](https://docs.rs#214)    /// // Parsing to digits from a slice
[215](https://docs.rs#215)    /// assert_eq!((42,2), i32::from_radix_10_signed(b"42"));
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    /// // Additional bytes after the number are ignored
[217](https://docs.rs#217)    /// assert_eq!((42,2), i32::from_radix_10_signed(b"42 is the answer to life, the universe and everything"));
[218](https://docs.rs#218)    /// // (0,0) is returned if the slice does not start with a digit
[219](https://docs.rs#219)    /// assert_eq!((0,0), i32::from_radix_10_signed(b"Sadly we do not know the question"));
[220](https://docs.rs#220)    /// // Signs are allowed
[221](https://docs.rs#221)    /// assert_eq!((-42,3), i32::from_radix_10_signed(b"-42"));
[222](https://docs.rs#222)    /// // Signs are allowed
[223](https://docs.rs#223)    /// assert_eq!((42,3), i32::from_radix_10_signed(b"+42"));
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    /// // Even on unsigned types.
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    /// assert_eq!((0,2), u32::from_radix_10_signed(b"-0"));
[226](https://docs.rs#226)    /// // Leading zeros are allowed
[227](https://docs.rs#227)    /// assert_eq!((42,4), i32::from_radix_10_signed(b"0042"));
[228](https://docs.rs#228)    /// ```
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    ///
[230](https://docs.rs#230)    /// # Return
[231](https://docs.rs#231)    ///
[232](https://docs.rs#232)    /// Returns a tuple with two numbers. The first is the integer parsed or zero, the second is the
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    /// index of the byte right after the parsed number. If the second element is zero the slice
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    /// did not start with an ASCII digit.
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    fn from_radix_10_signed(_: &[u8]) -> (Self, usize);
[236](https://docs.rs#236)}
[237](https://docs.rs#237)
[238](https://docs.rs#238)/// Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 10.
[239](https://docs.rs#239)/// Acts much like `FromRadix10Signed`, but performs additional checks for overflows.
[240](https://docs.rs#240)pub trait FromRadix10SignedChecked: FromRadix10Signed {
[241](https://docs.rs#241)    /// Parses an integer from a slice.
[242](https://docs.rs#242)    ///
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    /// # Example
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    ///
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    /// ```
[246](https://docs.rs#246)    /// use atoi::FromRadix10SignedChecked;
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    /// // Parsing to digits from a slice
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    /// assert_eq!((Some(42),2), u32::from_radix_10_signed_checked(b"42"));
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    /// // Additional bytes after the number are ignored
[250](https://docs.rs#250)    /// assert_eq!((Some(42),2), u32::from_radix_10_signed_checked(b"42 is the answer to life, the universe and everything"));
[251](https://docs.rs#251)    /// // (0,0) is returned if the slice does not start with a digit
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    /// assert_eq!((Some(0),0), u32::from_radix_10_signed_checked(b"Sadly we do not know the question"));
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    /// // While signed integer types are supported...
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    /// assert_eq!((Some(42),2), i32::from_radix_10_signed_checked(b"42"));
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    /// // Signs are allowed
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    /// assert_eq!((Some(-42),3), i32::from_radix_10_signed_checked(b"-42"));
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    /// // -0 is ok, even for an unsigned type
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    /// assert_eq!((Some(0),2), u32::from_radix_10_signed_checked(b"-0"));
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    /// // -1 is an Underflow
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    /// assert_eq!((None,2), u32::from_radix_10_signed_checked(b"-1"));
[261](https://docs.rs#261)    /// // Negative values for unsigned types are handled as `None`.
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    /// assert_eq!((None,3), u32::from_radix_10_signed_checked(b"-42"));
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    /// // Leading zeros are allowed
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    /// assert_eq!((Some(42),4), u32::from_radix_10_signed_checked(b"0042"));
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    /// // Overflow is indicated by `None`
[266](https://docs.rs#266)    /// assert_eq!((None, 3), u8::from_radix_10_signed_checked(b"256"));
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    /// assert_eq!((None, 4), i8::from_radix_10_signed_checked(b"+128"));
[268](https://docs.rs#268)    /// assert_eq!((None, 4), i8::from_radix_10_signed_checked(b"-129"));
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    /// ```
[270](https://docs.rs#270)    ///
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    /// # Return
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    ///
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    /// Returns a tuple with two numbers. The first is the integer parsed or zero if no digit has
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    /// been found. None, if there were too many, or too high dighits and the parsing overflowed.
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    /// The second is the index of the byte right after the parsed number. If the second element is
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    /// zero the slice did not start with an ASCII digit.
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    fn from_radix_10_signed_checked(_: &[u8]) -> (Option<Self>, usize);

# FromRadix10 in atoi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/atoi/3.1.0/atoi/trait.FromRadix10.html

`pub trait FromRadix10: `[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) {
    // Required method
    fn [from_radix_10](https://docs.rs#tymethod.from_radix_10)(_: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> (Self, [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html));
}## Expand description

Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 10

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/atoi/lib.rs.html#100)#### fn [from_radix_10](https://docs.rs#tymethod.from_radix_10)(_: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> (Self, [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/atoi/lib.rs.html#100)

#### fn [from_radix_10](https://docs.rs#tymethod.from_radix_10)(_: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> (Self, [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html))

Parses an integer from a slice.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use atoi::FromRadix10;
// Parsing to digits from a slice
assert_eq!((42,2), u32::from_radix_10(b"42"));
// Additional bytes after the number are ignored
assert_eq!((42,2), u32::from_radix_10(b"42 is the answer to life, the universe and everything"));
// (0,0) is returned if the slice does not start with a digit
assert_eq!((0,0), u32::from_radix_10(b"Sadly we do not know the question"));
// While signed integer types are supported...
assert_eq!((42,2), i32::from_radix_10(b"42"));
// Signs are not allowed (even for signed integer types)
assert_eq!((0,0), i32::from_radix_10(b"-42"));
// Leading zeros are allowed
assert_eq!((42,4), u32::from_radix_10(b"0042"));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#return)Return

Returns a tuple with two numbers. The first is the integer parsed or zero, the second is the index of the byte right after the parsed number. If the second element is zero the slice did not start with an ASCII digit.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

---

# FromRadix10Checked in atoi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/atoi/3.1.0/atoi/trait.FromRadix10Checked.html

`pub trait FromRadix10Checked: `[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) {
    // Required method
    fn [from_radix_10_checked](https://docs.rs#tymethod.from_radix_10_checked)(_: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> ([Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<Self>, [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html));
}## Expand description

Types implementing this trait can be parsed from a positional numeral system with radix 10.
Acts much like `FromRadix10`, but performs additional checks for overflows.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/atoi/lib.rs.html#134)#### fn [from_radix_10_checked](https://docs.rs#tymethod.from_radix_10_checked)(_: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> ([Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<Self>, [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/atoi/lib.rs.html#134)

#### fn [from_radix_10_checked](https://docs.rs#tymethod.from_radix_10_checked)(_: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> ([Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<Self>, [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html))

Parses an integer from a slice.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use atoi::FromRadix10Checked;
// Parsing to digits from a slice
assert_eq!((Some(42),2), u32::from_radix_10_checked(b"42"));
// Additional bytes after the number are ignored
assert_eq!((Some(42),2), u32::from_radix_10_checked(b"42 is the answer to life, the universe and everything"));
// (0,0) is returned if the slice does not start with a digit
assert_eq!((Some(0),0), u32::from_radix_10_checked(b"Sadly we do not know the question"));
// While signed integer types are supported...
assert_eq!((Some(42),2), i32::from_radix_10_checked(b"42"));
// Signs are not allowed (even for signed integer types)
assert_eq!((Some(0),0), i32::from_radix_10_checked(b"-42"));
// Leading zeros are allowed
assert_eq!((Some(42),4), u32::from_radix_10_checked(b"0042"));
// Overflow is indicated by `None`
assert_eq!((None, 3), u8::from_radix_10_checked(b"256"));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#return)Return

Returns a tuple with two numbers. The first is the integer parsed or zero if no digit has been found. None, if there were too many, or too high dighits and the parsing overflowed. The second is the index of the byte right after the parsed number. If the second element is zero the slice did not start with an ASCII digit.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*
